perspective:
Available to Sara Manuelito:

- I am Sara Manuelito, a speech-language pathologist. Shirley Whiteplume is a nurse, a long-time colleague, and close friend; we have worked together at a community health center for several years.
- At the funeral of a mutual patient, I observe Shirley’s somber demeanor and suspect she is deeply affected. I tell her I know this is hard and that I saw how much she cared. Shirley says it has been tough and she keeps wondering if more could have been done. I reply that we did everything we could and should remember the good care and joy we brought. She says I’m right, but it’s hard to let go.
- During a coffee break at work, I bring up the patient’s treatment decisions because I sense Shirley feels burdened. She says she feels responsible and wonders whether pushing for a different approach might have helped. I say we made the best decisions with the information we had and that it’s too heavy to carry alone. She appreciates it but says it’s hard to accept.
- I later observe Shirley being reserved and minimally expressive. In our office, I confront her, saying she’s holding back her feelings and it’s okay to be open. She says she isn’t sure she can and doesn’t want to seem unprofessional or weak. I say showing emotions doesn’t make her weak and is healthy among friends. She says maybe I’m right and she’ll try to be more open.
- Afterward, I feel my previous confrontation may have been too harsh. I apologize if I came on too strong. Shirley says it was a bit much, but she knows I meant well and appreciates the apology. I say I’m here for her however she needs. She thanks me and says we should keep talking; it helps.
- After some time, I notice Shirley seems to be doing better. I ask how she is feeling. She says she feels better thanks to our talks and my support. I suggest spending more time together outside work, maybe on the weekend. She says she would like that and suggests planning something for the weekend.

I have no access to Shirley’s private thoughts or feelings beyond what I observe and what she tells me.
